processing: Stems, leaves and flowers are dried whole, and today come from cultivated plants, as picking the wild plant in Bulgaria is banned.
harvest_season: Flowering stems are gathered when in flower, as with other Sideritis; the exact season varies with altitude and is rarely stated.
appearance_dry: Pale silvery-green, woolly stems with yellow flower heads.
appearance_wet: Soft grey-green stems and softened flower heads.
taste_profile: As with other mountain teas, expect a gentle herbal, slightly floral and sweet cup; honey and lemon are the usual additions.

brewing.notes: Traditionally simmered in a pot rather than steeped. Break the stems to fit. Serve with honey and lemon if you like.

vintage_note: Sold as dried bundles or cut herb with no vintages. Look for a label saying it is cultivated, since wild collection is prohibited in Bulgaria, and buy the most recent harvest available.
description:
Pirin tea, or mursalski chai, is the Bulgarian mountain tea, made from Sideritis scardica, a woolly Balkan herb of the mint family. It has no tea leaf and so no caffeine. The same species is sold in Greece as mountain tea.

It grows wild in the Pirin, Slavyanka and Rhodope mountains, at about 1,000 to 2,200 metres, and it is listed as critically endangered in the Bulgarian Red Book. That is why what you buy should come from cultivation, some of it from a selected Pirin population.

The traditional way is a decoction: boil the stems, leaves and flowers in a pot and serve with honey and lemon. The result is golden and gently herbal.

Treat any health promises on the pack as marketing, not clinical findings.
history:
Sideritis scardica was formally described in 1844; its older use as a herbal tea is not clearly dated. The Pirin name comes from the mountain.

The modern change is cultivation. Protection of wild plants has pushed the trade toward farmed plants, including those grown from a Pirin population.
